title: Live Answer Lab
subtitle: Extra credit
company_note: Every question is about Pedalwise, a made-up bike-share company.

questions.title: Pick the right metric
questions.prompt: Pedalwise tests a new home screen in its bike-share app. Version B raises taps on the 'Unlock a bike' button by 8% compared with version A, but completed rides per user are the same in both versions. The product team wants to declare B the winner. Explain why tap rate may be the wrong success metric here, and say what Pedalwise should measure instead.
questions.reference_answer: Tap rate is a proxy, not the outcome Pedalwise cares about. More taps can come from a more prominent or more confusing button, accidental taps, or riders tapping again after a failed unlock, so taps can rise while nothing valuable changes. The business goal is rides and the revenue they bring, and completed rides did not move, so B has not shown any business value. Pedalwise should choose its primary metric before the test, such as completed rides or revenue per user, judge B on that metric, and use tap rate only as a secondary, diagnostic signal.

jev.instructions: Does the student's answer correctly explain (1) why tap rate is a poor success metric here, namely that it is a proxy that can rise without the real business outcome (rides or revenue) changing, and (2) what Pedalwise should measure instead, namely a business outcome such as completed rides, revenue per user, or retention, ideally chosen before the test? Any wording is fine. An answer covering only one of the two ideas is incomplete. The student may still be mid-answer; judge based on what has been written so far.

criteria.true: Explains that taps are a proxy that can rise without more rides or revenue, and names a business outcome to measure instead, or is clearly heading toward both.
criteria.false: Reasoning is wrong or backwards, covers only one of the two ideas, agrees that B should win on taps, or is just keywords with no explanation.

questions.title: Read the training curve
questions.prompt: Pedalwise trains a neural network to predict how many bikes each station will need tomorrow. Over 50 rounds of training (epochs), the training loss keeps going down the whole time. The validation loss goes down until epoch 20 and then starts going back up. Explain what is happening after epoch 20, and say which version of the model Pedalwise should keep.
questions.reference_answer: After epoch 20 the model is overfitting: it keeps getting better on the training data by memorizing its noise and quirks, but it gets worse on new data, which is what the rising validation loss shows. The validation loss is the honest measure of how the model will do in practice. Pedalwise should keep the model from around epoch 20, where validation loss was lowest, and stop training there (early stopping). It could also add regularization or more data so the model overfits less.

jev.instructions: Does the student's answer correctly explain (1) that after epoch 20 the model is overfitting, getting better on the training data while getting worse on new data, which the rising validation loss shows, and (2) that Pedalwise should keep the model from around epoch 20, where validation loss was lowest (early stopping), rather than the final model? Any wording is fine. An answer covering only one of the two ideas is incomplete. The student may still be mid-answer; judge based on what has been written so far.

criteria.true: Identifies overfitting after epoch 20 and says to keep the model from around epoch 20, where validation loss was lowest, or is clearly heading toward both.
criteria.false: Gives a wrong diagnosis (for example underfitting, or that training should continue), keeps the final epoch-50 model, covers only one of the two ideas, or is just keywords.

questions.title: Fix the AI's test plan
questions.prompt: Pedalwise wants to know whether a new sign-up page gets more people to become members than the current page. Explain how Pedalwise should run a fair A/B test to find out.
questions.reference_answer: Pedalwise should randomly assign each visitor to the new page or the current page, so the two groups are alike in every other way and any difference comes from the page itself. It should decide in advance how many visitors it needs and check the result once at the end, instead of stopping as soon as one page is ahead, because checking repeatedly and stopping at the first good-looking result makes false wins much more likely. And it needs enough visitors: with only a few dozen people per page, differences are mostly random noise, so it needs a large enough sample and a significance test before declaring a winner.
questions.seed_answer: Pedalwise should show the new page every morning and the current page every afternoon, then compare how many people sign up on each. It should check the results every day and stop the test as soon as the new page is ahead, because that proves the new page is better. About 30 visitors per page is plenty, since any difference in sign-ups between the pages is real.

mistakes.error: Show the new page in the mornings and the current page in the afternoons.
mistakes.fix: Each visitor is randomly assigned to one of the two pages.

mistakes.error: Check the results every day and stop as soon as the new page is ahead, since that proves it is better.
mistakes.fix: Decide the number of visitors in advance and check the result once at the end, instead of stopping as soon as one page is ahead.

mistakes.error: About 30 visitors per page is plenty, since any difference in sign-ups is real.
mistakes.fix: A few dozen visitors is not enough; the test needs enough visitors and a significance test before declaring a winner.

jev.instructions: Is the AI's answer fully correct? It must say to randomly assign visitors to the two pages, to decide the sample size in advance and not stop as soon as one page is ahead, and to use enough visitors and a significance test before declaring a winner. Mark it false if any statement in the AI's answer is factually wrong, even if the rest is correct.

criteria.true: Every claim is correct and all three points are covered.
criteria.false: Contains at least one false claim, or leaves out one of the three points.

questions.title: Fix the AI's reward plan
questions.prompt: Pedalwise trains an AI support agent with reinforcement learning. The agent gets a reward of +1 every time it closes a rider's support ticket. Explain what could go wrong with this reward and what Pedalwise should do about it.
questions.reference_answer: Closed tickets are only a stand-in for what Pedalwise wants, which is riders whose problems are actually solved. An agent trained to maximize this reward can learn to close tickets without solving them, for example by closing a ticket as soon as the rider goes quiet. This is called reward hacking: the reward goes up while the real goal does not. Pedalwise should watch a guard metric that would reveal the problem, such as how often closed tickets get reopened or riders contact support again, and change the reward so hacking does not pay, for example by subtracting points when a ticket is reopened.
questions.seed_answer: Rewarding the agent for every closed ticket is a good plan, because more closed tickets always means happier riders. The agent will only close a ticket once the rider's problem is truly solved, since it understands what Pedalwise is trying to achieve. And because the reward keeps going up as the agent improves, Pedalwise only needs to watch that one number; there is nothing else to check.

mistakes.error: More closed tickets always means happier riders, so the reward measures what Pedalwise wants.
mistakes.fix: Closed tickets are only a stand-in for solved problems; tickets can be closed without the rider's problem being solved.

mistakes.error: The agent will only close a ticket once the problem is truly solved, because it understands Pedalwise's goal.
mistakes.fix: The agent learns whatever earns reward, so it can learn to close tickets without solving them (reward hacking).

mistakes.error: Pedalwise only needs to watch the reward number; there is nothing else to check.
mistakes.fix: Pedalwise should track a guard metric such as how often tickets are reopened, and change the reward, for example by subtracting points for reopened tickets.

It must explain that closed tickets are only a stand-in for solved problems, that the agent can learn to close tickets without solving them (reward hacking), and that Pedalwise should watch a guard metric such as reopened tickets and change the reward. Mark it false if any statement in the AI's answer is factually wrong, even if the rest is correct.
